Caddo

Caddo is a living Indigenous people with historical communities across the Red, Ouachita, Sabine, and Neches river regions. The Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is a contemporary tribal government formed from historically related communities; Caddoan language relationships do not make neighboring nations the same people. This Texas-focused guide distinguishes archaeological interpretation, written colonial records, Caddo oral histories, and current community work.

Read the sources [2] Caddo Nation of Oklahoma Language Program [8] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [14] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture; Howard Meredith [15] Oklahoma State Department of Education, Oklahoma Indian Education

Still unfinished

Seventeen distinct substantive works were inspected across Caddo Nation program material, Caddo-authored oral-history synthesis and testimony, archaeology and public history, a treaty text, and a historical governance document. This supports an accessible initial account of identity, homeland, archaeology, displacement, language work, and continuity. The collection remains unfinished because the post-removal era and current community/government perspectives are still thin, the region and named communities require more comparative review, and further primary and specialist works need direct inspection. The source count is a quantity measure, not completeness, endorsement, or community review.

Assessment recorded October 22, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The Caddo Nation official language page is a strong contemporary community source, but additional Nation-authored histories, cultural publications, and current government materials should be inspected.
  • The post-removal history, including the Civil War, allotment, federal policy, and the 1860–1902 period, needs deeper work with Caddo-centered and archival sources.
  • The three historical confederacies and named local communities are not fully surveyed here; terms vary across oral history, colonial records, and later scholarship.
  • The 1835 treaty is read as a printed statutory text only; signed manuscript, ratification files, later agreements, and implementation records were not separately inspected.
  • The Caddo Archeology Journal PDF was inaccessible to the text-review tool and remains an unread lead; this does not establish a paywall.
  • Archaeological interpretations of ancestral continuity and the northern Arkansas Basin remain debated; no fixed homeland boundary is asserted.
  • No present population figure, current fluent-speaker count, exhaustive community list, or claim of community endorsement is made.

Source & image record ↗ · Free to use — Smithsonian American Art Museum

George Catlin’s historical painting, dated 1846–1848 by the Smithsonian American Art Museum, depicts a mounted hunter and buffalo in the Cross Timbers of Texas. The item record names Caddo people, credits the painter and the Harrison gift, and explicitly marks the image Free to use. This is an outside artistic depiction, not a Caddo-made work, a photograph, or a survey of territory. The museum’s historical Catlin quotation is not adopted as factual synthesis. The complete available 2600×1873 digital frame and primary item/rights record were inspected; the web image is proportionally resized/recompressed, with no generated content or retouching. Cards and backdrops use CSS crops/overlays; the opened profile also shows the complete frame. This visual review adds no substantive source checks.

01

Names, related communities, and the Caddo Nation today

Historical sources use Caddo both for a particular northern community often called Kadohadacho and, more broadly, for several related Caddo-speaking communities. Caddo Nation language materials describe the historical Kadohadacho, Natchitoches, and Hasinai confederacies and emphasize that Pawnee, Wichita, Arikara, and Kitsai are linguistically related but remain culturally and historically separate Nations. The present Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is a contemporary government formed through 1930s reorganization; its 1938 constitution records one dated stage in that history, not today’s governing rules. The narrower Kadohadacho entry by Howard Meredith should be read for that community rather than generalized to every Caddo group.

Read the sources [2] Caddo Nation of Oklahoma Language Program [8] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [14] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture; Howard Meredith [15] Oklahoma State Department of Education, Oklahoma Indian Education

02

Homeland and place through time

Caddo historical communities are associated with river valleys across what are now northeast Texas, northwest Louisiana, southwest Arkansas, and southeast Oklahoma. The Caddo Homeland exhibit describes a large central homeland and a northern Arkansas Basin whose relationship to Caddo identity remains debated. It also explains that territories changed over time and that archaeological sites do not create fixed political borders. A separate Caddo oral-history synthesis describes three broad historical groupings and named villages using both community memory and colonial records. These regional descriptions document historical relationships; they do not define a present-day boundary or suggest that all Caddo people live in one place.

Read the sources [1] National Park Service [5] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [8] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [9] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [14] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture; Howard Meredith

03

Ancestors, archaeology, and what the evidence can show

Archaeological sequences trace distinctive Caddo pottery, villages, mound centers, agriculture, and long-distance exchange over many centuries. Researchers infer parts of that history from durable remains, but the timeline exhibit cautions that most ordinary lives and events leave little archaeological trace. The Texas Historical Commission’s Caddo Mounds account describes one important ceremonial and settlement center, not the whole Caddo world. A useful starting method is to compare archaeology with Caddo oral histories, language, written records, and later scholarship, while keeping uncertainty visible where those sources do not align.

Read the sources [3] Texas Historical Commission [6] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [7] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [10] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [12] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners

04

Contact, diplomacy, and records written by outsiders

Spanish, French, Mexican, and United States records describe encounters with Caddo communities, but they reflect the observers’ aims and assumptions. The Texas Beyond History research guide explains how missionary, travel, and government records can be useful while remaining selective and biased. Its Caddo Voices material, researched and written by enrolled Caddo historian Cecile Elkins Carter, combines oral histories with archival evidence and gives specific speakers and dates. Those accounts offer situated perspectives rather than one interchangeable story for every Caddo family or community.

Read the sources [7] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [8] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [9] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [12] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners

05

Treaties, displacement, and movement west

The 1835 treaty printed in the United States Statutes at Large records the cession agreement and related terms negotiated with named Caddo leaders. The instrument is evidence of the legal document and its signatories; it cannot by itself describe the different experiences of all Caddo communities or prove how every provision was carried out. Caddo Voices recounts movement from Louisiana into Texas, violence and loss of homes, and later movement to the Brazos area and west. Fallis Elkins’s 1973 family account and Sadie Bedoka Weller’s 1968 recollection are explicitly attributed testimony, not anonymous folklore. State and federal site histories add an institutional chronology of the 1855 reservation and 1859 removal, which should be read alongside those Caddo accounts.

Read the sources [3] Texas Historical Commission [9] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [11] Texas Beyond History; interview within the Created in Clay exhibit [13] United States Statutes at Large, hosted by GovInfo

06

Language, cultural continuity, and renewed practice

The Caddo Nation’s language program describes Caddo language as Hasinai in some contexts and situates language work within community history, gatherings, and cultural life. The program states that other Caddoan-language Nations are separate peoples. It also documents contemporary language-archive and learning work; language change or the loss of fluent speakers does not mean that Caddo people or culture have disappeared. The Texas Beyond History pottery exhibit connects ancient material evidence with Jeri Redcorn’s first-person account of learning and renewing Caddo pottery. A Texas Historical Commission exhibit developed with Caddo citizens and featuring artist Chase Kahwinhut Earles presents selected community knowledge about Caddo Mounds. These works are specific examples and do not stand for every citizen’s practice.

Read the sources [2] Caddo Nation of Oklahoma Language Program [4] Texas Historical Commission, in collaboration with Caddo citizens [10] Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners [11] Texas Beyond History; interview within the Created in Clay exhibit [16] U.S. Office of Indian Affairs / GovInfo [17] Texas Historical Commission and Caddo Nation of Oklahoma

Reviewed October 22, 2026 (America/Denver): 17 substantive works have actual-content inspection records; two supporting or out-of-scope references are excluded from the count. Links from a source bibliography and external embedded media are not treated as reviewed. The source set combines Caddo Nation program material, Caddo historian Cecile Elkins Carter’s attributed oral-history/archival synthesis, identified first-person testimony, government interpretation, archaeology education, a primary treaty printing, and a dated constitution. Their scopes and perspectives are labeled at the source cards. The language family is not a peoplehood shortcut: Caddo Nation materials state that Pawnee, Wichita, Arikara, and Kitsai are linguistically related yet distinct Nations. The Adai Caddo Indian Nation source is retained only as an explicit distinction and contributes no Caddo evidence or source count. The 1835 treaty and 1938 constitution are primary records for their own text and dates. They are not treated as complete accounts of community experience or current law/governance. The 2010-era OSDE figures are excluded from current claims. No new historical-map association was added. The NPS early-history page and Texas Beyond History exhibits contain map imagery, but map inspection, rights review, and a profile-specific association were outside this research batch.
